snippet.title: Why are Kenyan Gen Zs still protesting? | The Conversation | Focus on Africa - BBC Africa
snippet.description:
June 25 marks a turning point in Kenya’s history. What started in 2024 as youth-led protests against the Finance Bill grew into nationwide demonstrations. Led largely by Gen Z, protesters demanded justice for the fallen, an end to corruption, and real economic change. More than 60 lives were lost in the historic anti-tax protests.

In this episode of the Focus on Africa podcast, host Nkechi Ogbonna sits down with BBC reporters Akisa Wandera and Thomas Mukhwana. They break down why this leaderless youth movement refuses to back down and what this means for the future of Kenya.

We recorded this episode on 26th June – a day after protests brought Kenya's capital, Nairobi, to a standstill.

snippet.title: The 1892 Memphis Razor Murder Case of Alice Mitchell & Freda Ward That Shocked America
snippet.description:
On January 25, 1892, the city of Memphis became the stage for one of the most disturbing and controversial true crime cases in American history. Nineteen-year-old Alice Mitchell brutally killed her former fiancée, Freda Ward, in broad daylight on Front Street near the Mississippi River bluff. What followed was not just a murder trial, but a national reckoning with forbidden love, Victorian morality, and the limits of societal acceptance.

The two young women met at the prestigious Higbee School for Girls and formed an intense romantic bond that shocked 1890s America. When their plan to elope and live as husband and wife in St. Louis was discovered, family intervention separated them. Months later, rejection turned to obsession — and obsession turned deadly.

The trial that followed focused less on homicide and more on sanity. Within twenty minutes, a jury declared Alice mentally unfit and committed her to Western State Hospital, where she remained until her death in 1898. Meanwhile, Freda Ward was buried at Elmwood Cemetery in an unmarked grave, her voice overshadowed by sensational headlines.

This 10:39 deep-dive explores Victorian social norms, same-sex romantic friendships, courtroom strategy, and the tragic consequences of obsession in one of the earliest documented same-sex love murder cases in U.S. history.

snippet.title: Will visa-free travel change how Africans move across the continent? - BBC Africa
snippet.description:
Travelling across Africa is becoming easier for some, but for millions of Africans, crossing the continent can still mean expensive flights, visa requirements and long, indirect journeys. Just weeks after Togo announced visa-free entry for citizens of all African countries, adding fresh momentum to calls for freer movement across the continent, questions remain about how easy it really is for Africans to travel, trade and do business with one another. Daniel Dadzie examines why barriers to movement persist despite the ambitions of the African Continental Free Trade Area, and what still needs to change before a truly borderless Africa becomes a reality.

snippet.title: Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha's mother to head to the U.S. - BBC Africa
snippet.description:
The mother of Cape Verde's veteran goalkeeper Vozinha has arrived in the country's capital, Praia, to prepare for her trip to the United States. Ana Cândida Évora left her hometown of São Vicente on Wednesday night, accompanied by a lawmaker representing her district. The BBC understands Ms. Évora may fly to the U.S. between Friday and Saturday, ahead of Sunday's clash between Cape Verde and Uruguay in Miami. “I’m happy,” she told the BBC, expressing hope that everything will go smoothly.  “I’m taking a special energy to the Cape Verdeans there. We’re going to fight and shine on that pitch”, she added.
At the airport in São Vicente, she hugged family members and loved ones before heading to Praia.

snippet.title: Elizabeth Fenning: The Poison Trial That Sent an Innocent Woman to the Gallows
snippet.description:
In 1815 London, a young cook named Elizabeth Fenning was executed for a crime that still raises disturbing questions more than two centuries later. She ate the same meal that nearly killed an entire household—yet she alone was blamed, convicted, and sent to the gallows. How did a plate of dumplings become the foundation of one of Britain’s most controversial wrongful execution cases?

This 20-minute historical true-crime documentary explores the Elizabeth Fenning poisoning case, set against the backdrop of Georgian England, a society shaped by class hierarchy, fear of poison, and primitive forensic science. Through courtroom testimony, flawed arsenic tests, and social prejudice against domestic servants, this speech unpacks how circumstantial evidence outweighed reasonable doubt.

You’ll learn how early toxicology, unreliable medical science, and power imbalances within the legal system contributed to Fenning’s conviction. The video examines the Old Bailey trial, public outrage, failed appeals, and why her case became a catalyst for debates on capital punishment, forensic reform, and justice for the powerless.

If you’re interested in true crime history, wrongful convictions, British legal history, or cases that changed the justice system, this story is essential viewing. Elizabeth Fenning’s calm insistence on her innocence before execution forces us to confront a haunting question: was justice truly served, or did certainty replace proof?

Watch to the end and decide for yourself.
